lead: A receiver must pick one weak signal, amplify it, and hand a clean baseband copy to the demodulator. It cannot filter sharply at 900 MHz or 2.4 GHz, so it changes frequency to where good filters live. The superheterodyne receiver does this with a mixer and an intermediate frequency (IF). Direct conversion goes straight to zero frequency. Image-reject mixers cancel the unwanted mirror channel without a sharp RF filter. Every phone, Wi-Fi card and TV tuner uses one of these plans.
prereq: You need: 5.2 for noise figure and sensitivity, 5.3 for blockers and dynamic range, and 5.7 for mixer operation.

blocks.text: An antenna delivers many signals at once. The RF filter is a band-pass filter at the radio frequency (RF); it passes the wanted band and attenuates the image. The low-noise amplifier (LNA) boosts the signal with little added noise. The mixer multiplies the RF signal by the local oscillator (LO) and produces sum and difference frequencies. The difference is the intermediate frequency (IF). The IF filter selects one channel because a sharp filter at 45 MHz or 10.7 MHz is cheaper and more stable than a sharp filter at 900 MHz. The IF amplifier raises the level and the demodulator recovers the message.

blocks.where: f<sub>RF</sub> is the wanted radio frequency, f<sub>LO</sub> is the local oscillator frequency, and f<sub>IF</sub> is the intermediate frequency; all in Hz.

blocks.text: The mixer also responds to a second frequency, the image, that gives the same IF. For a high-side LO, f<sub>LO</sub> > f<sub>RF</sub> and f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub>. The image is f<sub>image</sub> = f<sub>LO</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub>. For a low-side LO, f<sub>LO</sub> < f<sub>RF</sub> and f<sub>image</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> − 2f<sub>IF</sub>. The image sits 2f<sub>IF</sub> away from the wanted signal.
f<sub>image</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub> (high-side LO); f<sub>image</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> − 2f<sub>IF</sub> (low-side LO)
blocks.where: f<sub>image</sub> is the image frequency; the sign follows the LO side.

blocks.text: The RF filter must reject the image before the mixer. If it does not, the image overlaps the wanted channel at IF and cannot be removed later.

A direct-conversion receiver sets f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub>, so f<sub>IF</sub> = 0. The mixer output is baseband. A low-pass filter selects the channel and the analog-to-digital converter (ADC) digitizes it. Some syllabi call this zero-IF. There is no image at a non-zero IF, because the wanted signal is at DC.

Four problems dominate. First, LO leakage radiates from the mixer or antenna and mixes with itself, producing a DC offset. Second, second-order distortion rectifies strong blockers to DC, adding another offset. Third, flicker noise (1/f noise) is large near DC and raises the noise floor for low baseband frequencies. Fourth, the I and Q paths have gain and phase mismatch, which leaves a residual image and increases error vector magnitude (EVM). DC offset can saturate the baseband amplifier, so zero-IF radios use calibration, AC coupling or offset cancellation.

An image-reject mixer cancels the image by using two mixing paths instead of a sharp RF filter. In the Hartley architecture, the RF input splits into two mixers. The LO drives one mixer at 0° and the other at 90°. Each mixer output passes through a low-pass filter. One path then gets a 90° phase shift, and the two paths are summed. The wanted signal adds in phase; the image adds in antiphase and cancels.

The Weaver architecture uses two quadrature mixing stages. The first stage translates to a low IF. The second stage translates to baseband with another pair of quadrature mixers and low-pass filters. Weaver avoids the wideband 90° phase shifter that Hartley needs, but it needs two well-matched LO paths. Only a few universities teach Weaver detail.

The image-reject ratio (IRR) is the ratio of wanted-signal power to image-signal power at the output. A perfect Hartley or Weaver mixer has infinite IRR. Real gain mismatch and phase mismatch leave a residual image. IRR of 30 dB to 40 dB is common; digital calibration can improve it. The mixer core, conversion gain and spurs belong to 5.7.

figure.caption: The superheterodyne chain takes 900 MHz through an RF filter and LNA, mixes with a 945 MHz LO to a 45 MHz IF, filters and amplifies the IF, then demodulates. The RF filter must stop the 990 MHz image before the mixer.

examples.question: A superheterodyne receiver receives a wanted signal at 900 MHz with an IF of 45 MHz and a high-side LO. (a) Find the LO frequency. (b) Find the image frequency. (c) A −20 dBm image blocker meets an RF filter that gives 30 dB rejection at the image, while the wanted signal is −80 dBm. Find the blocker power after the filter and compare it with the wanted signal.
steps: High-side LO means f<sub>LO</sub> is above f<sub>RF</sub>: f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub> = 900 MHz + 45 MHz = 945 MHz.

The image is on the other side of the LO: f<sub>image</sub> = f<sub>LO</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub> = 945 MHz + 45 MHz = 990 MHz. Equivalently f<sub>image</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub> = 900 + 90 = 990 MHz.
RF filter rejection subtracts in dB: P<sub>blocker,after</sub> = −20 dBm − 30 dB = −50 dBm.
Wanted signal is −80 dBm. The blocker is −50 − (−80) = 30 dB stronger than the wanted signal after the filter.
examples.answer: LO = 945 MHz, image = 990 MHz, blocker after the RF filter = −50 dBm, still 30 dB above the −80 dBm wanted signal.
examples.check:
f_rf = 900
f_if = 45
p_block = -20
rej = 30
f_lo = f_rf + f_if
f_img = f_lo + f_if
p_after = p_block - rej
print(f_lo)
print(f_img)
print(p_after)

traps: Using f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>IF</sub> for the image when the LO is high side. For a high-side LO the image is at f<sub>LO</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub>, which is f<sub>RF</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub>. A low-side LO puts it at f<sub>RF</sub> − 2f<sub>IF</sub>.
Saying the image spacing is f<sub>IF</sub>. The spacing is 2f<sub>IF</sub>.
Confusing DC offset with image in a direct-conversion receiver. The DC offset comes from LO self-mixing and second-order distortion, not from a non-zero IF image.
Assuming Hartley or Weaver cancels the image perfectly. Gain and phase mismatch leave a residual image, so IRR is finite.
Placing the IF filter before the mixer. A fixed IF filter cannot select a channel until after frequency translation.

quiz.q: Define image frequency in a superheterodyne receiver.
quiz.a: The image is the frequency that produces the same IF as the wanted RF after mixing: f<sub>image</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> ± 2f<sub>IF</sub>, with the sign set by high-side or low-side LO.

quiz.q: Why is the IF filter, not the RF filter, used for channel selection?
quiz.a: A sharp, narrow filter at a fixed low IF is cheaper, smaller and more stable than a tunable sharp filter at RF. The RF filter only needs to reject the image and strong out-of-band blockers.

quiz.q: A receiver has f<sub>RF</sub> = 2.4 GHz, IF = 100 MHz and a high-side LO. Find f<sub>LO</sub> and f<sub>image</sub>.
A zero-IF receiver's DC offset changes when a hand comes near the antenna. Explain the cause.
quiz.a: LO leakage reaches the antenna, reflects with a hand-dependent impedance, and returns to the mixer. It self-mixes to DC. The changing reflection changes the DC offset.
IRR is the ratio of wanted output power to image output power in an image-reject mixer, usually in dB.

quiz.q: Why does flicker noise matter more in zero-IF than in superheterodyne?
quiz.a: In zero-IF the wanted signal is at baseband near DC, where 1/f noise is large. A superheterodyne puts the signal at an IF far from DC, so flicker noise is less important.

quiz.q: A Hartley mixer gives −10 dBm wanted and −45 dBm image at its output. Find IRR in dB.
quiz.a: IRR = P<sub>wanted</sub> − P<sub>image</sub> in dB = −10 − (−45) = 35 dB.

quiz.q: Why can a direct-conversion receiver not rely on an IF filter to remove the image?
quiz.a: It has f<sub>IF</sub> = 0, so the wanted signal is at DC and there is no non-zero IF where an image sits. The image problem becomes the I/Q mismatch residual image and DC offset, not a separate RF image at 2f<sub>IF</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern handsets often use zero-IF or low-IF receivers with digital DC-offset and IQ calibration. Image-reject architectures appear in software-defined radio and low-power IoT front ends. Researchers work on N-path filters and mixer-first receivers that break the usual noise-linearity trade-off. Search for 'zero-IF receiver DC offset calibration', 'Hartley image-reject mixer IRR', and 'Weaver receiver architecture'.
